subject: Cooking
title: Coffee and Climate Change: A Shrinking Future
description: A short lesson to help you apply Coffee and Climate Change: A Shrinking Future.

hook.text: By 2050, climate change could destroy 50% of the land currently suitable for growing coffee. Your cup is at risk.

buildup.text: Arabica coffee needs 60–70°F, steady rainfall, and altitude. Warming temperatures push these zones higher and smaller.

discovery.text: Coffee leaf rust — a fungus thriving in warmer conditions — has already devastated crops across Central America.

twist.text: Wild coffee species in Ethiopia's forests may hold genetic keys to heat resistance — but deforestation threatens them.

climax.text: Scientists are crossbreeding resistant varieties, but time is short — it takes 25 years to develop a new coffee.

punchline.text: The morning coffee you take for granted is one of climate change's most vulnerable crops.

quiz.question: What percentage of coffee-growing land could be lost by 2050 due to climate change?

details.summary: Climate change could eliminate 50 percent of suitable coffee-growing land by 2050. Arabica coffee requires narrow temperature ranges and specific altitude conditions increasingly threatened by warming. Rising temperatures enable coffee leaf rust and berry borer infestations.
details.whyItMatters: Coffee is one of the crops most vulnerable to climate change. With over 125 million people depending on coffee for their livelihood, the stakes extend far beyond the cup.
takeaways: Up to 50 percent of coffee-growing land may be lost by 2050
Arabica requires narrow temperature and altitude conditions
Ethiopia could lose 60 percent of its coffee-growing areas

faq.question: Why is arabica coffee so vulnerable to climate change?
faq.answer: Arabica evolved in Ethiopian highland forests at specific temperatures between 60 and 70°F. It has narrow genetic diversity, making it less adaptable. Even small temperature increases reduce yields and quality.

faq.question: What is being done to save coffee from climate change?
faq.answer: Scientists are developing heat-tolerant varieties and crossbreeding with wild species. Some farms are planting shade trees to cool microclimates. Higher-altitude locations are being developed. The World Coffee Research organization coordinates global breeding programs.
